extracted.intended_audience: patent drafters, attorneys, and inventors (especially working on software and business-method inventions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on writing patent claim language to survive Alice/Mayo subject-matter eligibility review, with emphasis on software and business-method inventions. Focuses on claim wording, claim construction, and showing technical improvements or inventive concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo test (two-part analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Alice/Mayo test is a two-part analysis: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea, a law of nature, or a natural phenomenon (judicial exceptions); (2) if so, assess whether any element or combination of elements in the claim infuses an 'inventive concept' that is 'significantly more' than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this test as the framework for evaluating subject-matter eligibility. Draft claims with the two steps in mind: avoid language that reads as an abstract idea and include elements showing inventive concept or 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to a judicial exception (step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: First step: determine whether the patent claim is directed to an abstract idea, a law of nature, or a natural phenomenon (these are 'judicial exceptions' and not patentable by themselves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drafting claims that merely state an idea or goal without specifics. Identify whether the claim, as worded, would be characterized as one of these exceptions and reword to emphasize concrete application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive concept / 'significantly more' (step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Significantly more' requires that elements individually or as an ordered combination transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application. It is satisfied by an inventive concept beyond mere instruction to implement the abstract idea on a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show concrete technical improvements (improvement in another technology or functioning of the computer itself), meaningful limitations beyond generic computer implementation, novel/useful application, or a non-conventional/non-generic arrangement of known components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim language must concretely define the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim language should concretely define the invention and demonstrate practical application rather than merely stating an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use specific words/phrases that describe how the invention works and its tangible implementation; ground abstract ideas in real-world technical applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction — defining the meaning of words and phrases in a claim — is a critical, often preliminary, step in patent litigation and eligibility evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims and supporting specification so terms have clear, concrete meaning; anticipate how claim terms might be construed and ensure they point to a concrete implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate abstract ideas from concrete applications by articulating specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that merely states an idea or goal without specifics is likely to be seen as abstract; a claim that details a specific, inventive method or particular arrangement of components is more likely to be regarded as a concrete application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe how the invention achieves its goal step-by-step or by specific structure; include technical detail that ties the claim to a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid broad, sweeping language; tailor claims to specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: Overly broad claims risk encompassing abstract ideas and being rejected under Alice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit claim scope to the specific technical solution and distinguishing features of the invention. Use claim limitations that demarcate the concrete application and separate it from abstract characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame claims around technical problems and solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Alice, drafters should emphasize the technical problem addressed and the specific technical solution provided by the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In both claims and specification, explain the problem in the prior art and precisely how the invention solves it; tie claim elements to that technical solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight improvement over existing technology and practical application (USPTO guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO guidelines advise that claims should clearly convey the invention's improvement over existing technology and highlight practical application of any judicial exception involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state (in specification and where possible in claims) the technical improvement or functional enhancement and how it is achieved; eligibility depends on subject matter, not novelty/non-obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use non-generic, non-conventional arrangements or ordered combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventive concept can be shown by a novel, non-conventional, non-generic arrangement or an ordered combination of elements that transform an otherwise abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims that recite specific architectures, data flows, interactions, ordering, or other structural/functional details that are not merely conventional or generic computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cite and follow instructive case-law patterns (e.g., Diamond v. Diehr, Enfish, DDR Holdings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Case law shows what courts consider patent-eligible: Diamond v. Diehr upheld practical application of a formula; Enfish held that a specific software implementation on a general-purpose computer can be eligible; DDR Holdings upheld claims 'necessarily rooted in computer technology.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study successful cases to identify patterns: claims that focus on solving a technical problem, are rooted in computer technology, or claim a specific implementation tend to fare better under Alice. Use these examples to model claim phrasing and specification support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize technical nature rather than reliance on novelty/non-obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility under §101 focuses on subject matter (technical nature / concrete application), not on novelty or non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While novelty and non-obviousness remain important for patentability overall, ensure claim drafting addresses subject-matter eligibility by showing technical contribution and concrete implementation rather than relying on novelty arguments alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical drafting tactics: ground abstract ideas in real-world technical applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas should be grounded in real-world, technical applications — e.g., describe how an abstract idea is applied to solve a specific technical problem or improve technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete examples, system details, hardware/software interactions, performance improvements, and explicit statements of how the invention changes or improves technology to strengthen eligibility arguments.
